“That manifest regulation is what has pushed change in the past couple of years, because before that it was at least a bit more tolerable,” Schwenne said.
New regulations mandating electronic data exchange were formulated by the International Convention for the Safe Containers 2002 (CSC 2002), and are guided by the International Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods at Sea (IMO) Convention.
These have been propelled by events that have ignited worldwide worries about communication breakdowns and systemic intolerances, such as the 2005 terrorist attacks in Spain, during which containers filled with explosives were neutralized, and the 2003 chemical spill disaster in North Carolina, marked by the contamination of rivers due to leaking containers.
The shipping industry, which previously operated at a slow crawl, rightfully took a beating in the “blame game” that followed both events, Schwenne said.
Customs and the Coast Guard have intensely examined ocean carriers’ supply-chain systems, arguing that carriers, freight forwarders, and importers require improved computerized tools for managing cargo and sharing data. Carriers have faced criticism for their absence of a centralized computerized clearinghouse and a unified system linking all supply chain participants.
“The simple causes are the lack of, or broken, supply-chain management systems within the bigger corporations, so no one trusted the data because they didn’t have one system to trust and find it in,” Schwenne said.
Both ship and land-based communications have become tighter.
Last year, Kirby stated that APL’s import terminal in Dothan, Alabama used a method for manually printing electronic bills of lading and handling phone calls to generate the documents when shipping containers. Those paper shells were then taken to a “sister plating” facility to be stamped with the actual manifest information.
